clinicalPearls: A distinct subtype of renal cell carcinoma thought to arise from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct
Generally carries a more favourable prognosis than clear cell carcinoma of comparable stage
Often detected incidentally as a well-circumscribed solid renal mass on imaging
Histology shows large pale cells with prominent cell membranes and perinuclear haloes; the classic and eosinophilic variants are recognised
Multiple chromophobe tumours or oncocytic lesions should raise suspicion of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome
Sarcomatoid change, when present, denotes a markedly worse outlook
Distinguishing it from benign oncocytoma can be difficult on imaging and sometimes on biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is believed to originate from the intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct. It is characterised molecularly by widespread chromosomal losses affecting several chromosomes, producing a hypodiploid genome. The tumour cells accumulate abnormal microvesicles in the cytoplasm, giving the characteristic pale, flocculent appearance. Compared with clear cell carcinoma, it tends to be more indolent, although sarcomatoid dedifferentiation can transform it into an aggressive tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Eosinophilic solid and cystic renal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise the renal mass and stage disease
Renal mass biopsy where diagnosis will change management
Immunohistochemistry (including CK7 and other markers) to separate it from oncocytoma
Family and personal history assessment for Birt-Hogg-Dube features
Baseline renal function and staging investigations for larger or symptomatic tumours
redFlags: Rapid growth or new symptoms in a previously stable renal mass
Radiological features suggesting locally advanced or metastatic disease
Cutaneous fibrofolliculomas or lung cysts suggesting a hereditary syndrome
reference.prognosis: Localised chromophobe carcinoma generally has an excellent prognosis after surgical excision; outlook worsens substantially with higher stage, tumour necrosis or sarcomatoid transformation.
pitfalls: Confusing it with benign oncocytoma and either over- or under-treating
Missing an underlying Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome when tumours are multiple
Assuming an indolent course when sarcomatoid change is present
Relying on imaging alone to exclude malignancy in an oncocytic-appearing mass
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
